sections.html:
One department covers every step in Moore County, from listing and appraisal through billing and collection. Visit the Historic Courthouse at 1 Courthouse Square, Carthage, NC 28327, on a weekday between 8 am and 5 pm, or call 910-947-2255. Mail goes to Post Office Box 457 in Carthage.

The county's Tax page divides the work along the state statutes. Listing keeps ownership records and personal property accounts, and Appraising values land and buildings. Collecting has a current section for bills in their normal window and a delinquent section for past-due accounts.

  • Send the coupon from your bill by post, pay at the counter, or pay on the county's online page.
  • Phone 1-855-451-2620 with your bill numbers in hand.
  • Walk-in payers may use cash, checks or bank cards.
  • Credit cards and electronic checks run through InvoiceCloud, which adds a convenience fee for the cardholder.

Ask the Tax Department whether any town or district bill applies to your address in addition to the county bill.

The county's population reached an estimated 110,619 by mid-2025, a 10.9% rise from the 2020 base. Total housing units reached 52,979. For 2020-2024, owners lived in 76.4% of households, and half of owner-occupied homes were valued above $351,400.

At that price level, a small percentage error in your tax value repeats every year. Read your property record card against the house as you know it.

Each bill is due September 1. The grace period is set by G.S. 105-360: pay before January 6 and no interest applies; pay later and 2% is added through the end of January, then 0.75% for each month after.

January is also the listing season for personal property, including business equipment, which is listed every year. Real estate, once on the books, stays listed (G.S. 105-307). Statewide, owners list in January, with the window closing on the 31st unless an extension applies.

Selling in the fall does not erase that year's bill. Ask the closing attorney if it will be prorated or paid in full from your proceeds.

Revaluation here comes around every four years. The most recent one took effect January 1, 2023. The county has the next on its calendar for 2027, then every fourth year after, unless the market or state law calls for something different.

That is faster than the state floor of one reappraisal every eight years, and counties may shorten the cycle by resolution (G.S. 105-286).

Mass appraisal blends cost, market and income approaches and pins values to January 1 of the revaluation year. Values stay put between revaluations instead of tracking the market. An appraiser may still visit after a building permit, a parcel map change, or a recorded sale priced well away from the assessment. Permit data flows in from the county plus Aberdeen, Pinebluff, Pinehurst and Southern Pines.

Added heated floor area counts as an improvement, as do decks, porches, patios, storage buildings, pools and barns, and the owner is expected to report them.

Start with a signed written request or the county appeal form, sent to the Tax Department. For real estate you can appeal from each January 1 until the county's review board adjourns, a date advertised in the local newspaper.

Moore County appeal paths by property type
Property typeWhen to appealHow
Real propertyOpens January 1, ends at board adjournmentSigned request or appeal form, informal review first, then the board
Personal property, business or notThirty days counted from the bill dateSigned written request or personal property form
Registered motor vehicleThirty days counted from the bill dateSigned written request; pay the bill on time regardless

The burden is yours: show with cost, sales or income evidence from before the revaluation date that your value is out of line with nearby properties or above fair market value.

Lose at the board and you can go to the state Property Tax Commission by filing written notice within thirty days of the mailed decision (G.S. 105-290).

A permanent residence may qualify for one of three state programs, never two. In Moore County the application goes to the county tax office.

  • Elderly or disabled homestead exclusion: an owner who is 65 or older, or totally and permanently disabled, and within the income limit, has $25,000 or half of appraised value, whichever is larger, removed from the taxable amount (G.S. 105-277.1).
  • Disabled veteran homestead exclusion: $45,000 of value drops out of the bill, and neither age nor income is tested (G.S. 105-277.1C).
  • Circuit breaker: tax is held to 4% of income for owners at or below the limit and to 5% for incomes up to 150% of it, with the extra deferred as a lien (G.S. 105-277.1B).

The 2026 income limit is $38,800, and 150% of it is $58,200. File Form AV-9 with the county, ideally in the listing period; June 1 before the tax year begins is the last day the county must take it.

A sale or move triggers repayment of the circuit breaker deferral for the prior three fiscal years, so include it in the closing payoff.

sections.h2: Selling a house that still has tax due
sections.html:
Yes, though the tax stays with the parcel and gets paid at closing. Real property tax becomes a lien on the listing date (G.S. 105-355), and the county may enforce that lien through the foreclosure process in G.S. 105-374.

County court handles a tax foreclosure much like a mortgage foreclosure. The house goes to auction on the courthouse steps, but before confirmation the owner can still redeem by paying the tax plus penalties and costs.

Selling before that point usually costs less. Get a payoff from the Tax Department, check for an open town bill, and pass the total to your closing attorney.

sections.h2: How Moore County sets the value of a house
sections.html:
Every parcel is valued under the 2023 Schedule of Values adopted by the Board of Commissioners, using the features the house had on January 1 of the year in question. The appraiser records those features on a Field Review Document, and owners can pull that document or a shorter property record card from the county GIS site or from the Tax Department.

The land records team builds the ownership side from the paperwork that reaches the recorder's counter or the Clerk of Court, and it also keeps the parcel data that the GIS maps display. Mass appraisal means one set of standard methods is applied to a whole group of properties, then tested statistically. No single appraiser sets a price house by house.

  • Check the square footage, bedroom and bath counts and outbuildings on your card.
  • Look at what similar houses on your street are valued at.
  • Bring sales, cost or income evidence if you disagree, since the proof rests on you.
  • Remember that a recorded sale far from the assessment can trigger a visit.

For a seller, a clean card means fewer surprises when a buyer's agent compares your tax value to the contract price.

faqs.a: You can pay at the Carthage courthouse counter, through the mail, on the county website, or over the phone at 1-855-451-2620. The counter takes cash, checks and plastic, and card payments add a convenience fee.

faqs.q: What year did the last Moore County revaluation take effect?
faqs.a: January 1, 2023. The next one is scheduled for 2027, with four-year rounds after that.

faqs.q: How long can I contest a vehicle or personal property value?
faqs.a: The window is thirty days from the bill's date. Send a signed written request to the Tax Department, and pay a vehicle bill on time anyway so no late penalty builds.

faqs.q: Do Moore County values rise and fall with the market each year?
faqs.a: No. The county fixes value on the revaluation year's January 1 date and leaves it alone in between. New improvements can still draw an appraiser and change the figure.

faqs.q: Who accepts the elderly or disabled exclusion application?
faqs.a: The county tax office, on Form AV-9. It is best filed during January listing but is accepted up to June 1 before the new tax year starts, and a household can use just one of the three programs.
